result.summary: Pausanias finishes the night rites of Æsymnetes at Patræ, then tours the city's temples, statues and tombs, including those of Athene, Zeus, Apollo and Artemis Limnatis. He also tells how Preugenes brought Artemis Limnatis from Sparta.

scenes.title: Night rite of Æsymnetes
scenes.summary: Nine men and nine women tend the god Æsymnetes in his chest. At the festival, youths with corn crowns go to the Milichus, bathe, and put on ivy crowns.

scenes.title: Temples and market-place of Patræ
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes temples of Athene, the Mother, Zeus, Hera and Apollo, and the Odeum. He explains Apollo's ox skull with Homer's lines.

scenes.title: Artemis Limnatis and Preugenes
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the gate with golden effigies and the shrine of Artemis Limnatis. Preugenes brought her statue from Sparta, and he is honoured with a tomb.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo used in the quoted Iliad lines.
Cult title meaning 'of all the Achæans'.

notable_quotes.reason: Homer's lines on Poseidon and Apollo serving Laomedon, quoted to explain the statue.

analysis.text: The passage shows how cult practice changed, as sacrificial victims' corn crowns became offerings at the goddess's statue.
Pausanias links local monuments to Homer, Alcæus and contemporary builders like Herodes, showing Roman-era Greek civic pride.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes his Attica volume was written before Herodes finished the Athens Odeum, showing the work was composed over years.

language_notes.text: Refers to the Patræ legend that a youth and maiden were once sacrificed to Artemis; the corn crowns marked the victims. The Milichus is a local river.
Pan-Achæis means "of all the Achæans", an epithet of Athene as protector of the whole Achæan people.
"Next Olympian Zeus" means "next to"; brass is the translator's word for bronze.
"Filched" means stole; the story is the theft of Apollo's cattle by the infant Hermes.
Poseidon recalls that he and Apollo served the Trojan king Laomedon, building Troy's walls while Apollo herded cattle (Iliad 21).
The Galati are the Gauls, who invaded Greece in 279 BC; the Ætolians resisted them.
"Enterprize" is an old spelling of enterprise, meaning the undertaking.

context_notes.text: Attes (Attis) was the consort of the Phrygian Mother goddess Cybele, called Dindymene after Mount Dindymon.
Herodes Atticus was a wealthy Athenian benefactor of the second century AD; his Athenian odeum was named for his wife Regilla.
Æsculapius is the Greek god of healing.
Nemesis was the goddess of retribution; Aphrodite was the goddess of love.

literary_notes.text: The brief closing formula rounds off the rite and shows Pausanias' guidebook style, moving the reader on to the next sight.
Poseidon taunts Apollo, reminding the proud god that he once worked as a hired herdsman beside the walls built by Poseidon.
